Concrete Repair & Resurfacing · Oviedo, FL

Concrete Repair and Resurfacing in Oviedo

As of October 2026, concrete repair and resurfacing in Oviedo runs $3–$10 per sq ft (resurfacing) in the Florida market. The city added more than 1,200 residents between the 2020 census and mid-2025, so freshly poured work now sits beside driveways and walkways dating back to the 1997 median build year, old enough that a resurfacing decision is coming due.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

A driveway from Oviedo's median build year has had nearly three decades of Florida weather

Oviedo's typical home dates to 1997 (Census Reporter, Oviedo FL), old enough that a meaningful share of the city's original driveways and walkways show hairline cracking, a widened control joint or a chalky finish as ordinary wear rather than a warning sign. Whether a resurfacing job needs the full planning permit turns on whether it stays inside the existing footprint; Building Services at 407-971-5755 confirms the scope before material is ordered.

How a washed-out base shows up gradually, then all at once

Base erosion under an aging slab is usually slow: a small amount of sand or fines carried out through a hairline crack during each rainy-season storm, repeated over years until the void underneath is big enough to matter. A driveway can look stable for a long stretch and then develop a noticeable dip in a single wet season once the void finally collapses under traffic. On flatwoods soils common across both the Orlando and Suncoast service areas, where a seasonal high water table sits close to the surface for part of the year, that erosion process runs faster than it would on drier ground around Oviedo.

Seminole sits on shaky limestone ground, but not on the state's worst-claims list

Florida Geological Survey staff describe the state's sinkhole-prone terrain as shallow limestone sitting under a mix of sand and clay, a description that reaches into parts of Seminole County along with Orange, Lake, Marion, Citrus, Sumter and Volusia. Yet when the Florida Senate tallied where the claims actually land, Broward, Miami-Dade, Citrus, Alachua, Orange, Polk, Marion, Pinellas, Hillsborough, Pasco and Hernando accounted for over 88 percent of the sinkhole insurance claims filed statewide between 2006 and 2009, and Seminole's name is missing from that group entirely (Florida Senate Interim Report 2011-104). On an Oviedo driveway, a dip or crack is far more often the flatwoods water table working against loose fill than the sudden ground loss that list is built around.

Crack filling by the linear foot, not the square foot

A hairline or moderate crack that isn't tied to an underlying void gets treated as a linear repair rather than a surface one: a flexible filler or sealant worked into the crack itself, priced by the foot rather than the square foot, with Orlando-area figures running roughly 50 cents to $5 per linear foot depending on width and depth. That's a different job from resurfacing the whole slab, and it's meant for a crack that isn't actively moving or widening. A Oviedo driveway with a handful of scattered hairline cracks but a sound, level base is usually a crack-filling job, not a resurfacing one.

A worn driveway heading toward a resurfacing decision

Consider a 420 sq ft two-car driveway, original to a home built around the city's 1997 median, now showing a network of hairline cracks along its control joints. Resurfacing it at $3–$10 per sq ft (resurfacing) comes out somewhere between $1,260 and $4,200, cheaper for a plain broom finish and pricier once a decorative overlay is added. Choosing a full tear-out and repour instead moves the job into driveway-pricing territory and reopens both the city's planning permit and, if the apron is involved, its separate right-of-way review.

The resurfacing sequence: repair first, then the overlay

Resurfacing starts with pressure washing and sometimes an acid etch to open the slab's surface so the bonding agent can actually grip it, followed by patching any spalls or wide cracks before the overlay material ever goes down. The overlay itself gets applied, sometimes stamped or textured while it's still workable, then cured before a sealer finishes the job. Skipping the repair step and overlaying straight onto a dirty or flawed slab is how a Oviedo resurfacing job looks good on day one and shows every old flaw again within a year, right through the new surface.

A replaced panel that never quite matches the rest of the driveway

New concrete and old concrete age differently: the fresh panel starts out a slightly different shade, cures at its own rate, and can take years of sun exposure to weather close to the surrounding slab's color, if it ever fully matches. That's a cosmetic reality of cut-out-and-replace, not a flaw in the work itself, and it's worth setting that expectation with a Oviedo homeowner before the job starts rather than after. A mismatched panel that's structurally sound and correctly tied into the joint pattern is a successful repair even while it visibly reads as newer than what's around it.

Checking a repaired spot again after the first rainy season

The real test of any repair, mudjacking, polyjacking, resurfacing or a replaced panel, is whether it holds through a full wet season, not whether it looks right the week it's finished. A Oviedo homeowner who notices the same dip or crack returning after the rains have passed through is looking at evidence the underlying cause wasn't fully addressed, not a sign the repair method itself was wrong. That follow-up check costs nothing and catches a problem early enough to fix with another targeted repair rather than a full section replacement.

Frequently asked questions

Is cracking in a 1997-era Oviedo driveway something to worry about?

Usually not. Given the city's median home dates to 1997, a fine web of surface cracks and worn control joints on flatwork that age tends to be ordinary wear rather than a structural problem. A sudden, deep dip is the kind of thing worth a second look, a gradual hairline crack typically isn't.

Does Seminole County see sinkhole activity the way some nearby counties do?

Less than the counties the state's own claims data points to. Seminole shares the shallow-limestone geology found across parts of Central Florida, but it falls outside the eleven counties, led by Hernando, Pasco and Hillsborough, that generated most of the sinkhole insurance claims filed from 2006 through 2009.

Does a smaller resurfacing job skip Oviedo's permit process?

Sometimes, if it stays inside the slab's existing footprint; expanding the paved area pulls in the same planning review a new driveway needs. Calling Building Services before assuming a job is exempt avoids a surprise mid-project.
